title: Distributed Multi-objective Optimization in Cyber-Physical Energy Systems
authors: Sanja Stark, Emilie Frost, Marvin Nebel-Wenner
text:
A significant number of DER (DER) are introduced into the power system as a result of the energy transition. Many of the DER are based on renewable resources, such as wind and solar energy. In the future, these will account for the majority of the electricity supply while the generation from conventional power plants will decline. As a result, power generation will no longer be purely demand-driven but also depend on the weather, season, and time of day. At the same time, the growing number of electric vehicles, heat pumps, and storage systems can change consumption patterns. In particular, distribution grids require greater automation to effectively incorporate DER and manage the overall increasing system complexity, which calls for advanced ICT (ICT). ICT subsequently becomes an essential and integral component of the energy system, giving rise to a CPES.

The efficient and safe planning and operation of CPES can be described by various optimization problems with multiple objectives and constraints. Exemplary problems are managing energy systems on microgrid [1,2] or household level [3], optimal placement and sizing of DER [4,5] or system restoration [6,7]. The objectives include minimizing environmental effects or CO_{2} emissions, minimizing cost, minimizing power loss, and maximizing stability or reliability.

Due to potential conflicts between these objectives, one optimal solution usually does not exist but rather a set of trade-off or Pareto-optimal solutions, where the performance of one objective cannot be increased without reducing the other. Finding a Pareto front can be accomplished by population-based metaheuristics such as evolutionary or swarm-based methods. These algorithms search different regions of the solution space simultaneously and, with few modifications, can find a set of multiple non-dominated solutions in a single run [8]. Many different approaches from both of these algorithm classes have already been used in the context of energy system optimization, for example, particle swarm [9], slime mold [10], glow-worm [11] or grey wolf [12] optimization from the swarm-intelligence group and NSGA-2 [13,14,15,16] and MOGA [17] from the evolutionary group.

All these approaches use a central solver in which all necessary information is assumed to be available in one place. However, in the case of CPES, distributed control architectures have become more popular for certain tasks. In this case, multiple control elements have the joint responsibility for deciding on control actions to fulfill defined objectives [18]. A distributed control allows plug-and-play of DER, battery storages, or loads while at the same time being robust due to no single-point-of-failure [19]. Therefore, distributed architectures offer more flexibility and robustness compared with centralized ones [20]. Moreover, distributed approaches allow for preserving the privacy of DER and loads by storing technical details locally and only exchanging necessary information with other entities. This is particularly critical as it is common in CPES for some information to be only available distributed rather than collected at a central point.

To perform optimization processes with distributed architectures, a MAS (MAS) is a suitable choice [20]. MAS -based optimization in CPES has not only been studied in the context of microgrid management [1,2] but also, for example for the electricity market [21] or power system restoration [22]. We therefore extended the work from Bremer et al. in [23] and developed a fully distributed, agent-based algorithm to solve multi-objective optimization problems of CPES. Due to the diversity of optimization problems in CPES, we have ensured the extensibility and flexibility of the algorithm to allow easy adaptation to any problem at hand. Our goal is to provide a basic framework that allows to fully exploit the advantages of an agent-based multi-objective optimization – e.g. having different agents with different solving strategies, which can also be dynamically adapted during the optimization and for the specific problem, e.g., taking into account the computational power each agent has.

This paper has the following contributions:

- (1) Introducing MO-COHDA: a fully distributed agent-based multi-objective optimization algorithm, that is capable of solving distributed optimization problems with a potentially large number of decision variables where each entity only has limited control of one decision variable.

- (2) Evaluating the effectiveness of MO-COHDA by comparing it to NSGA-2 (NSGA-2) using multi-objective benchmark functions from the ZDT (ZDT) problem suite.

- (3) Showing with an example use case for scheduling a group of generation units with regards to three different objectives how MO-COHDA can be easily applied to real-life optimization problems in CPES.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives an overview of related work in the context of distributed multi-objective optimization. Section 3 describes the proposed multi-objective algorithm. Section 4 presents the evaluation of the algorithm with benchmark problems and Section 5 with a CPES problem. Finally, Section 6 gives a short summary of the results and describes possible future work.
